newsitem.title: UK: Church of England reviews ethical investment.
newsitem.headline: Church of England reviews ethical investment.

text.p: The Church of England said on Saturday it would review its ethical investment guidelines to focus more on the actions of individual companies.
The church currently observes blanket bans on investments in five sectors: armaments, gambling, breweries and distilleries, tobacco and newspapers.

"My amendment seeks to move the ethical investment policy away from looking just at industrial sectors to one which looks more closely at the companies themselves," said Robert Leach, the member who proposed the motion at the five-day General Synod in York, in northern England.
The motion was passed by a show of hands.
Worldwide, the church has investments worth a little less than 3 billion pounds ($5.1 billion), of which 56 percent is in equities, 30 percent in property and 14 percent in other assets.

Leach said refining the investment guidelines would remove some of the anomalies involved in banning companies purely by sector -- for example, the ban on alcohol-producing companies means the church cannot invest in communion wine.
It would also allow the church to take into account other factors than simply what the company makes.
Leach said increasing diversification in modern companies also made it harder to decide whether they fell into one of the banned categories or not.

He pointed out the arbitrary nature of a ban which bars the church from investing in gambling companies, while allowing it to hold a shareholding in Cadbury-Schweppes Plc, who are in turn major shareholders in Camelot Group Plc, the organisers of Britain's national lottery.

The Church of England's ethical investment working group was established in 1994 to bring together representatives of the main investing bodies of the church and examine ethical investment issues more closely.
It presented its first report in November but Saturday was the first time the working of the group was debated.

The support for moving towards closer scrutiny of individual companies and their practices was widespread in the synod and this was already partly reflected in the second report of the ethical investment working group, which pinpoints several companies over which it has had concerns.

Specifically it noted General Electric Co Plc, and said the group has held talks with the company about the exact nature of its defence work, after the church was recently criticised for investing in the international arms trade.

The report also mentioned oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group and concerns over its development policy in areas of socio-economic or environmental sensitivity, and Stagecoach Holdings Plc for the alleged breaching of its franchise in causing unacceptable delays to passengers over many weeks.
The church, which claims 80 million members worldwide and is Britain's state religion, has not withdrawn investment from any of these companies.
The synod meeting runs until July 15 and is to include discussions on other ethical issues, such as homosexuality within the church and the use of test-tube fertilisation.
